misconceptions.statement: A short password is fine if it has one capital letter and one number.
misconceptions.why: Students think a few special characters are what make a password strong, and ignore length.
misconceptions.fix: Length matters most. A long password or passphrase with many characters is much harder to guess than a short one with a few tricks.

probe.question: Which is stronger: 'Ravi@1' or 'blue-train-eats-seven-mangoes'?
probe.wrong_answer: Ravi@1, because it has capital letter, number and symbol.

misconceptions.root_belief: one visible feature decides the whole quality
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of user perceptions of password strength and security behaviour

misconceptions.statement: Replacing letters with similar numbers, like p@ssw0rd, makes a password very strong.
misconceptions.why: The change looks clever and complicated to the student.
misconceptions.fix: Attackers know common swaps like a to @ and o to 0. A common word with swaps is still easy to guess.

probe.question: Is 'p@ssw0rd' a strong password?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it uses symbols and numbers.

misconceptions.root_belief: looking complicated means being secure

misconceptions.statement: A password made from my pet's name and birthday is safe because only I know it.
misconceptions.why: Students feel personal means secret, forgetting others can learn or guess this information.
misconceptions.fix: Names, birthdays and phone numbers can be found from posts or guessed by people who know you. Avoid personal details in passwords.

probe.question: Is 'Moti2010' (pet name and birth year) a good password?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because only I know my pet's name and year.

misconceptions.root_belief: what is personal to me is secret from others
misconceptions.source_hint: research on user password choices and personal information

misconceptions.statement: Using one strong password for all my accounts is the safest and easiest way.
misconceptions.why: Students think a strong password is strong everywhere and find remembering many hard.
misconceptions.fix: If one site leaks the password, attackers try it on your other accounts. Use a different password for each important account.

probe.question: Aman uses one strong password for email, games and bank. Is that safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a strong password protects every account.

misconceptions.root_belief: one strong protection covers everything
misconceptions.source_hint: password reuse studies in security behaviour research

misconceptions.statement: It is fine to share my password with a close friend because friends are trustworthy.
misconceptions.why: Students link sharing with friendship and trust, and sharing games or streaming accounts is common.
misconceptions.fix: Passwords should stay private. A friend might leave it somewhere unsafe, use it by mistake, or fall out with you later.

probe.question: Your best friend asks for your email password to check something. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Give it, since a best friend can be trusted.

misconceptions.root_belief: trusting a person makes sharing secrets risk-free

misconceptions.statement: Closing the browser window logs me out of my account on a shared computer.
misconceptions.why: Students think closing a window ends everything, like closing a book.
misconceptions.fix: Many sites keep you logged in after the window closes. Always click log out, especially on school, cyber cafe or shared devices.

probe.question: After checking email in a cyber cafe, you close the browser tab. Is your account safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, closing the tab logs me out.

misconceptions.root_belief: closing something means ending it

misconceptions.statement: It is safe to tell an OTP to a bank or company caller who knows my name.
misconceptions.why: Students think someone who knows their name and details must be genuine.
misconceptions.fix: Real banks and companies never ask for your OTP. Anyone asking for it, even with your name, may be a fraudster.

probe.question: A caller says he is from your bank, knows your name and asks for the OTP. Do you tell him?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, he knows my name so he is from the bank.

misconceptions.root_belief: knowing some details proves someone is genuine

misconceptions.statement: An OTP is only dangerous to share if it is a very long number.
misconceptions.why: Students think only a password-like secret needs protection and a short code seems harmless.
misconceptions.fix: An OTP is a key for one action, such as a payment or login, and it can be used within minutes. Sharing it lets someone else do that action.

probe.question: A stranger asks for the 6-digit OTP you got. Is it harmless since it is short and expires soon?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is just a small number and expires, so it is harmless.

misconceptions.root_belief: small or short-lived things cannot cause big harm

misconceptions.statement: I must give my OTP or PIN to the bank caller, or my account will be blocked.
misconceptions.why: Fear and urgency in the call make students obey authority figures quickly.
misconceptions.fix: Banks never ask for OTP, PIN or CVV on call or message. Cut the call and contact the bank using its official number.

probe.question: A caller says your account will be blocked in 10 minutes unless you tell your PIN. What now?
probe.wrong_answer: Tell the PIN quickly to save the account.

misconceptions.root_belief: authority and urgency must be obeyed

misconceptions.statement: A link is safe if the message looks neat and has the company's logo.
misconceptions.why: Students judge trust by how professional the message looks.
misconceptions.fix: Fraudsters copy logos and designs easily. Check the full web address and avoid clicking links in unexpected messages.

probe.question: An SMS with a bank logo has a link to 'bank-kyc-update.xyz'. Is it safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it has the bank's logo so it is real.

misconceptions.root_belief: looks professional means it is genuine
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of how users judge phishing emails and websites

misconceptions.statement: Only strangers send phishing links, so a link from a contact is always safe.
misconceptions.why: Students assume danger comes only from unknown people.
misconceptions.fix: A hacked account or a forwarded message can send a harmful link from a friend. Be careful with unexpected links even from known people.

probe.question: Your cousin's WhatsApp sends 'Click to win free recharge'. Is the link safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it came from my cousin.

misconceptions.root_belief: danger comes only from strangers

misconceptions.statement: If a message says I won a prize or lottery, it must be real because they have my number.
misconceptions.why: Students think a message reaching them personally means they were truly selected.
misconceptions.fix: Scammers send the same message to thousands of numbers. A prize you never entered for is almost always a scam.

probe.question: You get an SMS saying you won Rs 10 lakh and must pay a small fee. What is true?
probe.wrong_answer: It is real because they sent it to my number.

misconceptions.root_belief: being contacted personally means it is meant for me

misconceptions.statement: Scams are only about money, so a request that does not ask for money is harmless.
misconceptions.why: Students link fraud only with payments.
misconceptions.fix: Fraudsters also steal passwords, personal details and photos, which can lead to account theft or blackmail later.

probe.question: A form asks only for your Instagram password to give free followers. Is it harmless since no money is asked?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they are not asking for money.

misconceptions.root_belief: harm only means one familiar kind of loss

misconceptions.statement: Once I set my profile to private, nothing I post can be seen or shared by anyone else.
misconceptions.why: Students think private means fully hidden from everyone.
misconceptions.fix: Private settings limit who can see posts, but followers can still screenshot or share them. Accept only people you know.

probe.question: Meena has a private account. Can her post still spread beyond her friends?
probe.wrong_answer: No, private means nobody else can ever see it.

misconceptions.root_belief: a label guarantees complete protection

misconceptions.statement: If I delete a post, it is gone from the internet forever.
misconceptions.why: On screen a deleted post vanishes, so students think it is erased everywhere.
misconceptions.fix: Others may have already saved, screenshotted or shared it. Information posted online can stay around, so think before posting.

probe.question: You post a photo and delete it after an hour. Can others still have it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, deleting removes it from everywhere.

misconceptions.root_belief: what I cannot see no longer exists
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of adolescents' understanding of digital footprints and online permanence

misconceptions.statement: Incognito mode makes me anonymous, so websites and my internet provider cannot see what I do.
misconceptions.why: The name and the spy-like icon suggest total invisibility.
misconceptions.fix: Incognito only stops the browser saving history and cookies on your device. Websites, your school or network, and your internet provider can still see activity.

probe.question: Using incognito at school Wi-Fi, can the school see which sites you visit?
probe.wrong_answer: No, incognito hides everything from everyone.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of user understanding of private browsing mode

misconceptions.statement: Incognito mode protects me from viruses and fake websites.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up being private with being protected.
misconceptions.fix: Incognito does not scan for harmful files or phishing. You can still get a virus or be tricked in incognito.

probe.question: Is it safe to download a strange file in incognito mode?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, incognito blocks viruses.

misconceptions.root_belief: private and safe mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: A website with a padlock or https is definitely trustworthy and genuine.
misconceptions.why: The padlock is often taught as a safety sign without explaining its limit.
misconceptions.fix: HTTPS only means the connection is encrypted. Fake sites can also use HTTPS, so check the web address too.

probe.question: A fake bank site shows a padlock. Is it safe to enter your details?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the padlock means it is safe.

misconceptions.root_belief: one sign alone proves everything is fine
misconceptions.source_hint: research on users' interpretation of browser security indicators

misconceptions.statement: Cyberbullying is only teasing and not serious since no one is physically hurt.
misconceptions.why: Students see only physical harm as real harm and treat online jokes as fun.
misconceptions.fix: Online bullying can cause fear, sadness and stress, and it can spread widely and be hard to remove. It is a serious harm.

probe.question: Classmates post mean memes of a girl. Is it just a joke?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, nobody is hurt physically so it is harmless.

misconceptions.root_belief: harm only counts if it is physical
misconceptions.source_hint: research on adolescent perceptions of cyberbullying and online harassment

misconceptions.statement: People who bully online using fake names can never be traced.
misconceptions.why: Students believe hiding a name means complete anonymity.
misconceptions.fix: Phones, apps and networks keep records, and police cyber cells can trace many offenders. Cyberbullying can be reported and punished.

probe.question: A user with a fake name keeps threatening a student. Can anything be done?
probe.wrong_answer: No, nobody can find out who it is.

misconceptions.root_belief: hiding one clue hides everything

misconceptions.statement: If someone bullies me online, I should reply in anger or stay silent and handle it alone.
misconceptions.why: Students fear being blamed or think replying will end it.
misconceptions.fix: Do not reply. Save screenshots as proof, block the person, report it on the app and tell a trusted adult. You can also use the helpline 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in.

probe.question: You get nasty messages every day. What is the best first step?
probe.wrong_answer: Send angry replies, or hide it and tell nobody.

misconceptions.root_belief: problems must be solved alone without help

misconceptions.statement: Forwarding someone's embarrassing photo is fine because I did not create it.
misconceptions.why: Students feel responsible only for what they make, not what they pass on.
misconceptions.fix: Sharing it spreads the harm and makes you part of the bullying. Do not forward it, and report it instead.

probe.question: A classmate's embarrassing photo reaches you. Is it okay to forward it to friends?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, I did not take it so I am not responsible.

misconceptions.root_belief: only the starter is responsible, not those passing it on

misconceptions.statement: Reporting an online fraud is useless because money lost can never be reported or recovered.
misconceptions.why: Students think reporting is pointless after the damage is done.
misconceptions.fix: Report quickly on helpline 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in and inform the bank. Fast reporting can help freeze or recover money.

probe.question: Money was fraudulently taken through UPI an hour ago. Should you report it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the money is gone and nothing can be done.

misconceptions.root_belief: once something has happened, it cannot be changed

misconceptions.statement: If I use OTP login, I do not need a strong password.
misconceptions.why: Students think the OTP is a complete replacement for the password.
misconceptions.fix: Two-step verification uses both. A strong password adds a layer, and if the OTP is stolen, the password still protects you.

probe.question: An account has OTP login. Can its password be '1234'?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the OTP will protect it anyway.

misconceptions.root_belief: one protection removes need for others
